content.title: About
content.content: Reduced‑fat cookie brownie is a soft, aromatic treat that blends the classic chocolatey flavor of a brownie with the light texture of a cookie. The product is not covered with icing (NS — no icing) and is suitable for those watching their fat intake.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Brownies originated in the United States in the early 20th century as a "cake‑like" dessert.
Fat reduction is achieved by replacing part of the butter with plant oils and apple puree.
Cookie brownies are often used as a base for dessert tarts and ice‑cream sundaes.
Without icing, the natural cocoa and vanilla flavors shine through more clearly.
In many markets, similar items are sold in the "healthy" or "light" snack aisles.

items.title: Lower Calorie Content
items.content: Reduced fat means fewer calories per serving, helpful for weight management.

items.title: Rich in Antioxidants
items.content: Cocoa provides flavonoids that help combat oxidative stress.

items.title: Source of Dietary Fiber
items.content: Whole‑grain flour often used in the recipe adds beneficial fiber.

items.title: Contains Magnesium
items.content: Magnesium supports normal muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Low in Trans Fats
items.content: Absence of partially hydrogenated oils makes the product heart‑friendlier.

items.title: Gluten Allergy
items.content: The product contains wheat flour and is not suitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Sugar Content
items.content: Despite reduced fat, the recipe still includes a moderate amount of sugar.

items.title: Caffeine
items.content: Cocoa naturally contains small amounts of caffeine, which may affect sensitive individuals.

items.title: Food Additives
items.content: Some batches may contain emulsifiers or stabilizers that can trigger reactions in sensitive consumers.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the cookie brownie as a snack on its own, crumble it into yogurt or ice cream, or use it as a layer in desserts. For a softer texture, keep it at room temperature in an airtight container.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place in a sealed package. For longer shelf life (over 2 weeks) keep refrigerated to maintain freshness and prevent drying out.

content.title: About
content.content: The “Breakfast Biscuit” crackers are light, dry biscuits designed for a quick morning meal. They are made from wheat flour, vegetable oils, and a modest amount of sugar, giving them a mild taste and crisp texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first commercial batch was launched in 1998.
The formula often includes vitamin B1 (thiamine) to support energy metabolism.
Crackers are packaged in individual serving packets, making them popular for travel.
They are commonly enjoyed with milk, yogurt, or fruit puree.

items.title: Quick source of energy
items.content: Carbohydrates in the crackers are rapidly absorbed, providing an immediate energy boost in the morning.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: B1 and B2 vitamins help support metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Low fat content
items.content: Compared with many breakfast options, these crackers have a moderate fat level.

items.title: Convenient and portable
items.content: Lightweight and ready‑to‑eat, they suit busy lifestyles.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Crackers contain wheat flour and are not suitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Some varieties may contain added sugar, which should be considered by individuals with diabetes.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: They can raise blood sugar quickly, so pairing with protein or fiber is recommended.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Crackers can be eaten plain, dipped in milk, added to yogurt, or used as a base for spreads such as cottage cheese, avocado, or low‑fat cheese.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place in a tightly sealed package. For extended storage, keep in the refrigerator to prevent spoilage.

content.title: About
content.content: Chocolate soft drink is a non‑alcoholic carbonated beverage flavored with chocolate, containing carbonated water, sugar (or sugar substitutes), cocoa mass, flavorings and preservatives. It offers a sweet, slightly bitter chocolate taste combined with refreshing fizz.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first chocolate‑flavored soda appeared in the United States in the early 1970s.
The chocolate‑and‑fizz combination is especially popular in Japan, where it is often served in specialty cafés.
Both natural cocoa powder and caramel coloring are used to achieve the characteristic brown hue.
Several brands offer a diet version sweetened with low‑calorie sweeteners.
Carbonation enhances perceived sweetness, making the drink seem less sugary than it actually is.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Cocoa mass is rich in flavonoids, which may support cardiovascular health.

items.title: Quick energy boost
items.content: Sugar and caffeine (in some formulas) provide a rapid increase in energy levels.

items.title: Mood improvement
items.content: Chocolate stimulates the release of serotonin and endorphins, which can improve mood.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Regular versions contain a lot of sugar, which can contribute to weight gain and increase the risk of tooth decay.

items.title: Caffeine
items.content: Some variants contain caffeine, which may be undesirable for children and caffeine‑sensitive individuals.

items.title: Cocoa allergy
items.content: A small number of people may be allergic to cocoa components.

items.title: Carbonation
items.content: Excessive consumption of carbonated drinks can cause stomach discomfort and heartburn.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve chilled straight from the refrigerator. It can be used as a base for cocktails, added to ice cream for a chocolate float, or mixed with milk for a creamier texture.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep the cap tightly sealed to preserve carbonation. Discard if the taste or smell changes.

spinach-fresh-cooked-no-added-fat.title: Spinach, fresh, cooked, no added fat

content.title: About
content.content: Spinach is a leafy vegetable from the Amaranthaceae family. When cooked without added fat it retains most of its vitamins and minerals, offering a mild flavor and tender texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Spinach provides more than 20% of the daily value of vitamin K, essential for blood clotting.
Short boiling reduces the oxalate content compared with raw leaves.
Spinach has been used in cuisine since ancient Rome and ancient China.
There are over 50 spinach varieties, differing in leaf color and taste.
Spinach is often called a "green superfood" because of its dense nutrient profile.

items.title: Rich in vitamin K
items.content: Vitamin K is crucial for bone health and proper blood coagulation.

items.title: Source of vitamin A and folate
items.content: Vitamin A supports vision, while folate is important for cell division and fetal development.

items.title: Contains iron and magnesium
items.content: These minerals aid energy metabolism and muscle function.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Lutein and zeaxanthin protect the eyes from age‑related degeneration.

items.title: Low‑calorie food
items.content: One cup of cooked spinach contains about 40 kcal, making it an excellent choice for weight management.

items.title: Oxalates
items.content: High oxalate levels may contribute to kidney stone formation in susceptible individuals.

items.title: Medication interactions
items.content: Vitamin K can reduce the effectiveness of anticoagulants such as warfarin.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Rarely, some people may experience an allergy to spinach.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cooked spinach without fat can be served as a side dish, added to soups, omelets, pasta, or salads. A squeeze of lemon, a touch of garlic, or a pinch of spices enhances its flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh spinach in the refrigerator in a perforated bag or a container lined with a damp paper towel for up to 3–5 days. Cooked spinach should be stored in an airtight container in the fridge and used within 2 days.
